questions.q: Which of the following options best describes the features of a collaborative design team?
options: Leader directed, common skills among the group, responsive to feedback
Leader directed, various fields of professional expertise, responsive to feedback
Shared understanding of the project, common skills among the team, cooperative decision-making process
Shared understanding of the project, various fields of professional expertise, cooperative decision-making process
questions.explanation: A collaborative team shares a common understanding of the project, brings together varied fields of expertise, and makes decisions cooperatively rather than being directed by a single leader. This is exactly the collaboration the episode highlights in P.E Nation and Tin and Ed.

questions.q:
A web design company has introduced a collaborative design approach.

Which of the following is likely to take place?
options: Team members multi-task in each project.
A project manager directs the development of ideas.
Each design project is allocated to all team members.
Team members work together to discuss and share ideas.
questions.explanation: Collaborative design relies on team members working together to discuss and share ideas, pooling varied expertise in cooperative decision-making. A single manager directing ideas describes a directed rather than collaborative approach.

questions.q: A design team works best when
options: tasks are allocated to individuals based on expertise.
the designer’s work flow is structured and organised.
design teams work in direct competition with each other.
team members always work independently towards a goal.
questions.explanation: Effective collaborative design teams allocate tasks according to each member's expertise so the right skills are applied to each part of the project, just as Pip Edwards and Claire Tregoning split P.E Nation's work by their complementary strengths. Constant competition or working independently undermines the cooperation that makes a team productive.

questions.q: According to the episode, which statement best captures the nature of a designer's work?
options: A lone genius who works in isolation, relying on flashes of inspiration
A problem-solver who combines creativity and technology, is shaped by influences such as culture, history, environment and personal experience, and often works collaboratively
An artist whose work is primarily self-expression and answers only to the artist
A technician who applies fixed rules to a single set of materials and tools
questions.explanation: The episode's four-point skeleton is that designers come from a range of fields, solve problems by combining creativity and technology, are influenced by culture, history, environment and personal experience, and often work collaboratively. It explicitly rejects the 'lone genius' image; self-expression answering to the artist describes art, not design.

questions.q: Which scenario is an example of the OVERLAP of design professions, rather than their interaction?
options: Industrial designers, engineers, ergonomists and marketers all contributing to the design of one car
An architect designing furniture as well as buildings, because the design process is adaptable
A graphic designer emailing files to a client for feedback
A manufacturer producing the final product from the designer's drawings
questions.explanation: Overlap is one designer crossing into another's territory because the underlying design process is adaptable — the episode's example is an architect designing furniture (and graphic designers Tin and Ed making installations). Different professions working side by side on one car is interaction, not overlap.

questions.q: Which of the following is an EMERGING design career created by new technology, rather than a traditional pathway?
options: Industrial and product designer
Fashion and textile designer
User-experience (UX) and user-interface (UI) design
Architect and interior designer
questions.explanation: The episode splits careers into traditional pathways (industrial, graphic, fashion, architecture, engineering) and emerging fields created by technology — UX and UI design, sustainability consulting and digital fabrication, with even newer ones like augmented and virtual reality design. The other three options are traditional pathways.

questions.q: From memory, list the four points the episode uses to describe the nature of a designer's work.
keyPoints: Designers come from a range of fields — fashion, industrial, graphic, multimedia and more.
They solve problems by combining creativity and technology (the idea plus the means to make it real).
They are influenced by culture, history, environment and personal experience.
They often work collaboratively — with engineers, clients and manufacturers.
questions.explanation: These four points are the skeleton of any 'describe the nature of a designer's work' answer. If you recalled all four in syllabus language, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: In your own words, what separates a band-four 'describe a designer' answer from a band-six one?
keyPoints: A band-four answer is biography: it lists who the designer is and what products they made.
A band-six answer describes the nature of their work and processes in syllabus language.
It covers the needs or opportunities they responded to, how they apply and adapt the design process, who they collaborate with, and the influences shaping their work.
The weak answer says what; the strong answer says how, and ties it to the design process.
questions.explanation: Describing the process — not just the products — is the single most important move from this episode, and it is exactly what outcome H1.2 rewards in Year 12.

questions.q: Explain what is meant by the interaction and overlap of design professions. (3 marks)
questions.modelAnswer: Interaction refers to different design professions working together on a single project — for example industrial designers, engineers, ergonomists and marketers all contributing to the design of a car. Overlap refers to the boundaries between professions blurring, because the design process is adaptable to almost any situation, so a designer can work beyond their original field — for example an architect designing furniture, or trained graphic designers like Tin and Ed producing physical installations. The two are not the same: interaction is professions working together, while overlap is the boundaries between them blurring.

criteria.descriptor: Defines interaction as different design professions working together on a single project, with an example.
Defines overlap as the boundaries between professions blurring, with an example.
Links overlap to the adaptability of the design process and distinguishes it from interaction.

questions.explanation: The trap is treating the two words as the same thing; the marker wants the distinction — professions working together versus boundaries blurring — and the overlap linked to the adaptability of the design process.

questions.q:
A team of designers is working together on a design project.

Describe how information storage devices could be used to support the teamwork and collaboration of these designers.
questions.modelAnswer: Information stored in digital form on devices such as computer hard drives, USB memory sticks and CDs can be emailed to team members quickly and easily for sharing ideas and gathering feedback, unlike bulky paper-based storage. External hard drives let designers carry larger and greater quantities of files between locations. Files held on a computer network can be password protected, with members assigned different permissions such as read-only or the right to modify. Documents can also be uploaded to the 'cloud' for web-based storage, allowing designers in diverse geographical locations to upload, comment and edit collaboratively in real time, even with virtually unlimited storage space.

criteria.descriptor: Clearly describes how teamwork and collaboration of the designers is supported by information storage devices
Outlines different ways that teamwork and collaboration of the designers is supported by information storage devices
Outlines how teamwork and collaboration could be supported by information storage devices
Identifies features of teamwork and collaboration and/or information storage devices
Identifies a feature of teamwork and collaboration or an information storage device

questions.explanation: This real HSC question rewards concrete links between storage devices (local drives, networks, the cloud) and the collaboration the episode stresses — shared files, controlled permissions and real-time editing across locations.
